item.title: How do we know when invasive species control strategies work?
item.author: Pearse IS, Barnett DT, Beaury EM, Blumenthal DM, Bradley BA, Buonaiuto D, Corbin JD, Dukes JS, Nebhut A, Sofaer HR, Sorte CJB, Vilà M, Petri L.
item.description:
Controlling invasive species is costly and difficult but can have major ecological, economic, and health benefits. Researchers commonly compare the efficacy of specific control methods. However, invasive species control programs vary greatly in overarching goals and often occur over large areas, long timeframes, and varied environmental and social contexts. The success of these programs likely hinges on factors including organizational structures, concurrent restoration activities, geographic and temporal scope of control, and the invasive species' biology. To enable assessment of the relative influence of these common features, we propose clearer definitions of success in invasive species control and explicit comparisons among control programs. Post hoc assessment of existing programs' success will complement system-specific studies to guide strategies that work in real-world situations…

item.title: Behavioral diversity knowledge shortfall in biodiversity conservation.
item.author: Jarić I, Blumstein DT, Prchalová M, Cordero-Rivera A, Ladle RJ, Aleklett K, Arlinghaus R, Berger-Tal O, Bertram MG, Brose U, de Oliveira Caetano GH, Couzin ID, Diniz-Filho JAF, Firth JA, Futamura R, Gaston KJ, Hortal J, Karban R, Keith SA, Lessa T, López-García P, Marske KA, Martins EP, Moreira D, Ord TJ, Pengal P, de Oliveira Roque F, Sbragaglia V, Signaroli M, Smederevac-Lalić M, Snijders L, Wan KY, Westrelin S, Wong BBM, Monk CT.
item.description:
Behavior is a critical but underexplored component of biodiversity, often overlooked in conservation science, ecological restoration, and biodiversity management. We argue that behavioral diversity needs to be formally recognized as a distinct facet of biodiversity, given its critical value as a reservoir of adaptive potential, and that current gaps in knowledge should be acknowledged as what we formally define to be a behavioral diversity knowledge shortfall. Present knowledge shortfalls need to be confronted by establishing standardized behavioral diversity indicators, harnessing recent technological developments and large databases, building capacity, promoting interdisciplinary collaboration, and setting research priorities. item.title: Parasites in the meta-ecosystem landscape: hidden connectors and disruptors.
item.author: Selbach C, Henriksen EH, Paterson RA, Poulin R, Frainer A.
item.description:
The meta-ecosystem framework explains spatial flows of organisms, materials, and energy across ecosystem boundaries. Parasites play crucial roles in these processes, yet they remain absent from meta-ecosystem models. Using examples from terrestrial and aquatic environments, we illustrate how parasitic organisms act as central connectors or disruptors of the flow of organisms, nutrients, and energy across ecosystem boundaries via four key mechanisms: parasite-induced host movement, behavioural changes that increase cross-ecosystem predation, host mortality, and parasite avoidance behaviour. These examples highlight the central role of parasites in driving and regulating nutrient and energy flow from catchment-to-coast, and we outline a pathway for improved integration of these parasite-mediated processes into the meta-ecosystem framework.

item.title: Plant reproductive palaeobiology: a window into long-term reproductive dynamics.
item.author: Prohaska A, Rosbakh S, Nielsen R, Czech L, Macias-Fauria M.
item.description:
Reproductive dynamics strongly influence genetic diversity and population structure, with important implications for ecological interactions and evolutionary trajectories. However, our understanding of plant reproductive dynamics remains limited due to the scarcity of long-term studies. Here, we propose a conceptual and methodological framework for tracking plant reproductive dynamics over long timescales using pollen, plant spore, and seed records preserved in sedimentary archives. The analysis of counts, morphology, and DNA from fossil propagules enables reconstruction of reproductive patterns over centennial to million-year timescales. When integrated with other palaeoproxies, these records provide insights into environmental drivers and eco-evolutionary consequences of reproductive dynamics. item.title: Trees alone do not make forests.
item.author: Fischer GA, Zhang J, Smith P, Gale SW.
item.description:
Forest restoration is often evaluated based on tree cover, while other dimensions of ecosystem recovery remain depleted, simplified, or incompletely reassembled. We define this mismatch as hollow forest syndrome and propose deficit profiles and an adaptive framework to diagnose recovery gaps, identify limiting processes, and guide restoration toward whole-forest recovery.

item.title: Back to seedlings: rethinking the slow-fast continuum across tree life stages.
item.author: Umaña MN, Norden N, Hurtado-M AB.
item.description:
Forest dynamics have traditionally been interpreted through the lens of adult trees, yet most mortality occurs during the seedling stage, shaping future forests. A central assumption in ecology is that demographic trade-offs, such as the slow-fast continuum, operate consistently across ontogeny. However, increasing evidence challenges this view. Seedlings experience high pest-driven mortality, strong environmental filtering, and stochastic variation in dispersal and microsite conditions, which can decouple early-life performance from adult demography. We synthesize recent developments suggesting that seedling trade-offs may either reflect a scaled-down version of adult dynamics or diverge into alternative axes, such as the recruitment-stature axis. item.title: Socioeconomics and biodiversity in cities: moving beyond patterns to mechanisms.
item.author: Reynolds C, Awoyemi AG, Batáry P, De Toni A, Findlay SJ, Fletcher RJ, Gwedla N, Muvengwi J, Naidoo S, Shackleton C, Venter ZS, Chamberlain D.
item.description:
Socioeconomic status-biodiversity associations are widely reported in cities. However, most studies remain correlational and cannot distinguish whether socioeconomic status drives biodiversity change, biodiversity shapes socioeconomic outcomes, or whether observed patterns reflect biodiversity gains versus losses. We propose a unifying framework organizing established mechanisms from diverse urban research into four hypothesized causal pathways: (A) investment-driven biodiversity enhancement, (B) disinvestment-driven biodiversity degradation, (C) biodiversity-driven socioeconomic improvement, and (D) biodiversity loss reinforcing socioeconomic decline. item.title: Precipitation timing matters for flowering communities.
item.author: de Manincor N, Fisogni A, Rafferty NE.
item.description:
Flowering times have long been a harbinger of the changing seasons and, more recently, of a changing climate. Among the cues that trigger flowering, precipitation timing has been relatively little-studied. Tsafon et al. show that the timing of precipitation shapes flowering in complex ways. Much work remains to disentangle this complexity.

item.title: From 'magic traits' to diversification mechanisms.
item.author: Wang Y, Freckleton RP.
item.description:
Species richness is markedly uneven across the tree of life, and traits have long been invoked to explain this pattern. Expanding phylogenetic and trait datasets enable broader comparisons, but trait-diversity associations alone do not reveal how differences in richness arose. We argue that such associations should be reframed as process hypotheses about three non-exclusive processes: lineage origin, access to ecological or geographic opportunity, and persistence. Mixed trait-diversity associations are expected when the same trait influences multiple processes whose relative contributions vary across contexts. item.title: From species richness to interaction architecture.
item.author: Eisenhauer N, Yi H, Wildermuth B.
item.description:
Biodiversity research has long focused on the number and identity of species, but recent advances suggest that ecosystem functioning depends on how species are connected. Predicting the consequences of biodiversity loss in the Anthropocene will therefore require moving beyond inventories of species toward a predictive ecology of interaction networks.
